title: Cyber Defenders Unit 4 · Tricks and tricksters (3-5)

items.q: A message says: 'Hurry! You won a prize! Reply in five minutes to claim it!' What is a clue that it is a trick?
choices: It arrived on a screen
It rushes you and offers a prize you never tried to win
It uses words you can read
It says hello at the start
items.why: Every message arrives on a screen and uses words. The clues are the rush and a prize for a contest you never entered.

items.q: A message from someone you do not know says: 'Tell me your mailbox key so I can fix your account.' What is the biggest clue?
choices: It is a short message
It mentions a mailbox
It asks for your key, which real games never do
It came during the day
items.why: Real games and helpers never ask for your key. A short message or a mention of a mailbox is not a clue by itself.

items.q: A message asks for your passphrase. What should you do?
choices: Reply and ask why it needs it
Tap its link to check first
Share it with a friend
Do not reply, do not tap, and show a trusted adult
items.why: Replying, tapping or sharing gives the trick what it wants. Do not reply, do not tap, and show a trusted adult.

items.q: A trick promises a shiny prize if you just tap its button. Which motive is behind it?
choices: The key-hunter, who wants into your mailbox
The prize-faker, who dangles a reward to get your tap
The giggler, who wants a big reaction
The forwarder, who wants you to share it onward
items.why: A shiny prize that only needs a tap is bait. That is the prize-faker, who dangles a reward to get your tap.

items.q: You do not reply to a trick message. Which two tricksters does that stop, and why?
choices: The key-hunter gets no key, and the giggler gets no reaction
The message turns into a safe one
Your mailbox closes forever
The trickster forgets your name
items.why: Silence starves two motives at once: the key-hunter never gets a key, and the giggler never gets a reaction.

items.q: A trick sends a silly, teasing message again and again, hoping you will answer back angrily. Which motive fits it best?
choices: The key-hunter, who wants your key
The prize-faker, who dangles a reward
The forwarder, who wants you to share
The giggler, who wants a reaction
items.why: Teasing again and again, hoping you will answer back angrily, is fishing for a reaction. That is the giggler.

items.q: Which poster is most likely a trick, because its promise is too good to be true?
choices: A town shop poster listing its opening times
A poster promising free gems to the millionth visitor
A poster for a school play on Friday
A poster asking you to return a lost scarf
items.why: Free gems for the millionth visitor is too good to be true. Opening times, a school play and a lost scarf are ordinary news.

items.q: You see an amazing claim on a poster. How can you check it before you believe it?
choices: Share it and see what happens
Believe the poster with the biggest words
Ask a trusted adult and check a trusted site
Wait for the poster to change
items.why: Big words and sharing do not make a claim true. A trusted adult and a trusted site can check it.

items.q: Why is sharing a fake post a problem in itself?
choices: It uses up your sharing for the day
It is only a problem if it has pictures
Fake posts are too heavy to carry
It passes the trick to friends, who may believe it and be fooled
items.why: Sharing a fake carries the trick to friends who trust you, and they may be fooled. That is the harm in itself.
